style: Narrate in a deep, slow, ominous true-crime documentary voice, with dramatic pauses:
sections: In 1950, a ship sailed past San Francisco and sprayed something into the fog. Eight hundred thousand people breathed it in. Nobody told them. Nobody asked them.
That's story three. And honestly? It's not even the darkest one in this video. These are three true stories your history teacher skipped.
Christmas Eve, 1926. New York City. A man stumbles into Bellevue Hospital, screaming that Santa Claus is chasing him with a baseball bat.
He's not alone. Within days, dozens of people are dead. Not from bad moonshine. From poison. And the poison was put there on purpose... by their own government.

Here's what happened. During Prohibition, bootleggers stole industrial alcohol and turned it back into drinkable liquor. So federal officials ordered manufacturers to add more poison. Methyl alcohol. Kerosene. Benzene. They knew people would drink it. That was the point.
New York's chief medical examiner, Charles Norris, was furious. He called it, quote, our national experiment in extermination.

By the time Prohibition ended, the poisoning program is estimated to have killed at least ten thousand Americans. One supporter shrugged it off. Anyone who drinks it, he said, is committing deliberate suicide.
The government poisoned the drinks. But at least those people knew drinking was a risk. The women in the next story were told their poison was good for them.
New Jersey, 1917. The best job a young woman could get: painting watch dials with a miracle paint that glowed in the dark. The secret ingredient was radium.
To keep the brush tips sharp, they were taught one technique. Lip. Dip. Paint. Hundreds of times a day, they put radium in their mouths.
Their bosses said it was harmless. So they painted their nails with it. Their teeth. They walked home at night, glowing like ghosts.
But down the hall, the company's own scientists handled the same material with lead screens and tongs.
Then the teeth started falling out. In 1922, a dial painter named Mollie Maggia went to her dentist with a sore jaw. He touched it gently... and the bone came away in his hand.
She died that year, at twenty-four. Her death was blamed on syphilis. A lie that protected the company, and destroyed her name.
Five dying women finally sued. The company stalled, hoping they'd die before the verdict. They won in 1928, and their fight helped build the worker safety laws that protect you today.
Radium has a half-life of sixteen hundred years. Those women are still radioactive in their graves. Right now.
A company poisoned its workers. But what happens when the target is an entire city?
September, 1950. For about a week, a US Navy ship sits off the coast of San Francisco, pumping a mist into the famous fog.
Inside that mist: billions of bacteria. The military wanted to know how vulnerable a city would be to a germ attack. So they simply attacked one. Their own.
The test was a success. Nearly all of the city's eight hundred thousand residents inhaled the bacteria. The Navy believed it was harmless.
Days later, doctors at a Stanford hospital saw something so rare they wrote a paper about it: eleven patients with the same strange infection. One of them, a man named Edward Nevin, died.
His family didn't learn the truth for over twenty-five years. In 1977, the Army admitted it. And San Francisco wasn't the only one.
Two hundred and thirty-nine secret tests. Over twenty years. Including bacteria released into the New York City subway, at rush hour.
The Nevin family sued. They lost. The court ruled the government couldn't be held responsible.

A poisoned bottle. A glowing paintbrush. A fog that wasn't just fog. Each time, someone in power decided ordinary people were an acceptable cost. And each time, it only ended because someone refused to stay quiet.
But these three were eventually admitted. The story in this next video was buried for much longer. Click it, and I'll see you there.
